analysis.one_liner: Forces the government to take nuclear plant waste to a Nevada storage site by a deadline.
analysis.headline: The Senate Energy Committee reported the bill favorably on March 29, 1996 with 29 Senate cosponsors, but the Senate never voted on it before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the 1982 Nuclear Waste Policy Act to order the Department of Energy to take title to spent fuel from commercial nuclear power plants and move it to a temporary storage facility at the Nevada Test Site, with permanent disposal at Yucca Mountain. It let utilities settle all their disposal obligations with a one-time fee, shielded the federal government from lawsuits over missed deadlines, barred the EPA from setting the repository's radiation standards, and narrowed environmental review and court access. The Senate Energy Committee approved it, but the full Senate never voted.
analysis.who_benefits: Nuclear utilities that hold spent fuel at their reactors gain the most: the bill orders DOE to accept the waste by November 30, 1999, transfer title to the government, and, once the one-time fee is paid, releases the utility from any further financial obligation for storage or disposal [S3]. Waste transport and disposal contractors gain mandated "private sector participation" in moving and managing the fuel [S3]. Nuclear customers get the argument that waste moves off crowded reactor sites, and states along transport routes get planning funds and training assistance [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Orders DOE to take title to, transport, and store the commercial nuclear industry's spent fuel at a Nevada interim facility by November 30, 1999, ending the industry's waiting game after the government missed its 1998 contract deadline.
Provides that payment of a one-time fee relieves a utility of any further financial obligation to the federal government for long-term storage and permanent disposal of its waste.

Requires DOE to use private industry 'to the fullest extent possible' for transportation and to engage private-sector participation throughout the program, opening the multi-billion-dollar operation to contractors.
Lets utilities meet waste-acceptance commitments as a prerequisite for renewing their reactor operating licenses, reducing regulatory uncertainty for plant owners.

analysis.who_pays: Ratepayers keep paying the 1.0 mil-per-kilowatt-hour fee into the Nuclear Waste Fund that finances the program [S3]. Taxpayers fund DOE's construction of the interim facility, rail line, and transport fleet. Nevadans bear the direct burden: the state is designated as host over any objection, with the EPA stripped of its authority to set the repository's radiation protection standard and the environmental review barred from considering alternative sites [S3, S4]. Communities along rail and highway routes bear the transport risk, and courts of appeals get exclusive jurisdiction over challenges, with no power to stop construction before final rulings [S4].

drawbacks.text: Strips the EPA of any role in setting radiation protection standards for the repository, replacing existing standards with a statutory 100-millirem limit and barring the licensing regulations from considering them — a weaker standard for future generations living near Yucca Mountain.

Declares route designation, site selection, and facility construction 'preliminary decisionmaking activities' that require no environmental impact statement, and bars the eventual review from considering alternative sites, designs, or even whether the facility is needed.

Sends all civil actions to the federal courts of appeals with original and exclusive jurisdiction, prohibits courts from enjoining construction of the rail line or storage facility before final decisions, and makes the Secretary's benefits-agreement decisions unreviewable by any court.

Overrides Nevada's objection to hosting the facility: the state and its counties can accept payments without that being treated as consent, but they cannot stop the siting, and the bill directs land withdrawals and a rail corridor through Lincoln County as a matter of law.

Shields the United States from any financial liability if DOE misses the acceptance deadlines, which in practice shifts the risk of the program's delays onto the utilities' ratepayers and host communities rather than creating a real enforcement mechanism.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real problem: spent fuel is piling up at dozens of reactor sites while DOE has already missed its contractual acceptance deadline, and utilities keep suing for the delay. But this version solves the problem almost entirely on the industry's terms — a host state designated over its objection, EPA locked out of setting the safety standard, environmental review barred from weighing alternatives, courts stripped of power to pause construction, and the government shielded from the very liability its missed deadlines created. A stronger bill would have compensated for delay, preserved independent safety standard-setting, and kept meaningful review open to the communities bearing the risk.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared the Senate Energy Committee and was placed on the Senate calendar, but the Senate never brought it to a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.

narrative.text: Senator Larry Craig introduced the bill on September 25, 1995 with a bipartisan list of original cosponsors including Democrats Hollings, Heflin, Robb, Levin, Nunn, and Shelby.
The bill gathered 29 cosponsors in total — 24 Republicans and 5 Democrats — and the Energy and Natural Resources Committee held hearings on it on December 14, 1995.

On March 29, 1996 the committee, chaired by Senator Frank Murkowski, reported the bill favorably with a substitute amendment and placed it on the Senate Legislative Calendar as Calendar No. 360; the reported version moved the acceptance deadline from January 31, 1998 to November 30, 1999 and added a shield against federal liability for missed deadlines.
The bill's last recorded action was sponsor remarks in May 1996; the Senate never voted on it, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nevada and communities along the proposed transport routes were spared a facility and waste shipments they opposed. Nuclear utilities did not get the acceptance schedule, title transfer, or full liability release they sought, and remained stuck with waste at reactor sites.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nevada residents and communities near transport routes

for.name: Sen. Larry Craig
for.role: U.S. Senator from Idaho, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it through introduction and committee consideration.

for.name: Sen. Frank Murkowski
for.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill favorably to the Senate with a substitute amendment and placed it on the legislative calendar.

for.name: 24 Senate Republicans and 5 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including original cosponsors such as Thurmond, Lott, Helms, Hollings, Nunn, Levin, and Robb.

against.name: Sen. Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Led Senate opposition to the Yucca Mountain interim storage plan and used Senate procedure to keep the bill from reaching a floor vote.

against.name: Sen. Richard Bryan
against.what_they_did: Opposed the bill as a designated-host mandate against Nevada and supported blocking floor action.

against.name: President Bill Clinton
against.what_they_did: Threatened to veto nuclear waste legislation that forced interim storage on Nevada, signaling the bill would not become law in that form.

sides.party_line_note: Support was heavily Republican — 24 of the 29 cosponsors — though 5 Democrats signed on, while opposition centered on Nevada's two Democratic senators and no roll-call vote was ever taken.

industries.note: The bill forces the government to take title to and haul away their spent fuel by a fixed date, releases them from all further disposal obligations once a one-time fee is paid, and shields them from having to keep waste at reactor sites indefinitely. The cost falls on ratepayers and on the host state and transport corridors, which get weaker standards and less court access in return.

industries.industry: Radioactive waste transport and disposal contractors
industries.note: The bill mandates private-sector participation 'to the fullest extent possible' in transporting and managing the waste and requires DOE to run the program 'like a private business,' guaranteeing a new multi-billion-dollar federal workflow. Communities along the routes get training and planning funds, but also the shipments themselves.

industries.industry: Engineering and construction firms (repository, rail, and storage facility builders)
industries.note: The bill directs construction of an interim storage facility, a rail spur from Lincoln County, and intermodal transfer capability at Caliente, with rules that let site preparation begin before licensing. The work is funded by the ratepayer-financed Nuclear Waste Fund.
